While this architecture has been stable and reliable, it has become increasingly difficult to maintain as our product complexity grows. ### Pain Points 1. **Over-fetching data in mobile apps**: Mobile clients must request full resource objects even when only a few fields are needed, consuming unnecessary bandwidth and battery. 2. **Multiple API calls needed for dashboard views**: Complex dashboard views require 5-10 separate API calls to gather all necessary data, leading to: - Increased latency - Poor user experience - Higher server load 3. **Frontend teams complaining about rigid data structure**: The REST structure forces frontend developers to adapt to predefined schemas, making it difficult to: - Implement new features quickly - Customize data views per client - Optimize for specific use cases ### Stakeholders This decision impacts the following teams: - **Frontend teams**: Will gain flexibility in data fetching - **Mobile team**: Will benefit from reduced data transfer and improved performance - **DevOps**: Will need to plan for migration and monitoring changes - **Product managers**: Will see faster time-to-market for new features ### Constraints - Decision must be made before Q2 planning - Must maintain backwards compatibility for 6 months to avoid breaking existing integrations ## Decision **We will adopt GraphQL as our new API architecture** while maintaining the REST API for backwards compatibility during a 6-month transition period. The migration strategy involves: 1. Deploying a GraphQL layer alongside the existing REST API 2. Gradually migrating internal services to GraphQL queries 3. Deprecating REST endpoints in a controlled manner after 6 months 4. Providing migration tools and documentation for all stakeholders ## Rationale ### Why GraphQL? 1. **Efficient Data Fetching**: Clients request exactly the data they need, eliminating over-fetching and under-fetching issues. 2. **Single Endpoint**: Reduces the number of API calls needed for complex views from 5-10 to 1, significantly improving latency. 3. **Strong Schema Definition**: Provides a centralized contract that benefits frontend teams with better tooling and type safety. 4. **Flexible Evolution**: New fields and relationships can be added to the schema without breaking existing clients. 5. **Better Developer Experience**: Query builder tools and introspection capabilities reduce frontend development time. ### Why Not Other Options? - **gRPC**: Too low-level for public-facing APIs; better suited for internal microservice communication - **SOAP**: Outdated and overly verbose; GraphQL is more modern and flexible - **Keeping REST**: Doesn't solve the core problems of over-fetching and rigid structures ### Cost-Benefit Analysis | Factor | REST (Current) | GraphQL (Proposed) | |--------|---------------|-------------------| | Data efficiency | Low (fixed responses) | High (custom queries) | | API calls for dashboard | 5-10 | 1 | | Frontend flexibility | Low | High | | Migration effort | N/A | Medium-High | | Maintenance overhead | Low | Medium | ## Alternatives Considered ### 1. Continue with REST API **Pros:** - No migration effort - Existing documentation and knowledge - Lower immediate cost **Cons:** - Doesn't solve over-fetching problem - Performance issues will worsen - Frontend teams will continue to be frustrated - Competitive disadvantage ### 2. REST with Pagination and Filtering Improvements **Pros:** - Lower migration risk - Quick implementation - Some bandwidth savings **Cons:** - Still requires multiple API calls - Doesn't solve rigid data structure problem - Limited flexibility for complex queries - Temporary solution ### 3. GraphQL Federation **Pros:** - Scalable for microservices - Multiple backends can be federated - Industry standard approach **Cons:** - Higher complexity - Requires learning curve - More initial setup time ### 4. GraphQL with REST Proxy Layer **Pros:** - Maintains backwards compatibility - Gradual migration possible - DevOps can manage transition **Cons:** - Additional infrastructure layer - Potential performance overhead - More maintenance **Selected Approach**: Option 4 (GraphQL with REST Proxy Layer) provides the best balance of innovation and stability for our team. ## Implementation Plan ### Phase 1: Preparation (Weeks 1-4) 1. **Setup GraphQL Infrastructure** - Install and configure Apollo Server or similar - Set up schema definitions - Configure type system 2. **Schema Development** - Map existing REST endpoints to GraphQL types - Define resolver functions - Implement field-level permissions 3. **Documentation** - Create GraphQL schema documentation - Write migration guide - Prepare developer workshops ### Phase 2: Development (Weeks 5-12) 1. **Build GraphQL API** - Implement core resolvers - Add validation and error handling - Set up caching layer 2. **Integration Testing** - Test with internal services - Performance benchmarking - Security audit 3. **Documentation** - API documentation - Migration tools - Best practices guide ### Phase 3: Pilot (Weeks 13-16) 1. **Internal Deployment** - Deploy to staging environment - Migrate one internal service - Collect feedback 2. **Stakeholder Review** - Present to Product managers - Get DevOps approval - Mobile team validation ### Phase 4: Migration (Weeks 17-28) 1. **Gradual Rollout** - Enable GraphQL for new features - Document deprecated REST endpoints - Monitor usage patterns 2. **Support** - Provide migration assistance - Answer technical questions - Collect feedback ### Phase 5: Transition Complete (Weeks 29-32) 1. **Full Cutover** - Switch internal services to GraphQL - Deprecate REST endpoints - Update documentation 2. **Monitoring** - Track performance metrics - Monitor error rates - User satisfaction surveys ### Timeline Summary | Phase | Duration | Key Deliverables | |-------|----------|------------------| | Preparation | 4 weeks | Infrastructure, Schema, Docs | | Development | 8 weeks | GraphQL API, Testing | | Pilot | 4 weeks | Staging Deployment, Feedback | | Migration | 12 weeks | Gradual Rollout, Support | | Transition | 4 weeks | Full Cutover, Monitoring | ## Risks and Mitigations | Risk | Impact | Likelihood | Mitigation | |------|--------|------------|------------| | Performance degradation | High | Medium | -
